items.title: Fermented milk may have held ritual power in Neolithic Denmark
items.snippet: Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

items.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
items.snippet: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

items.snippet: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. items.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
items.snippet: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
items.snippet: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
items.snippet: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. items.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
items.snippet: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

items.title: Uterine pressure guides head-to-tail axis formation in mouse embryos
items.snippet: During animal development, the establishment of the three primary body axes—head-to-tail (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral and left-right—is essential for building a proper body structure. A fertilized egg, initially a single cell, undergoes repeated cell divisions to form a multicellular structure called an embryo, and body axes are formed within the embryo.
